cases.response:
Lo que describes suena agotador: cuarenta y cinco años sosteniendo a otros, y ahora una pregunta que no sabes responder. Y cada vez que intentas poner un límite, la culpa llega tan fuerte que parece confirmar que no tienes derecho a hacerlo.

Me pregunto si la culpa está midiendo algo distinto de lo que tú crees. Puede que no te diga que hiciste algo malo, sino que estás rompiendo un acuerdo antiguo, uno que aprendiste muy pronto: que tu valor dependía de lo disponible que estuvieras. Por eso decir "no" se siente como traicionar a alguien, aunque lo que haces sea simplemente existir como persona con necesidades. La culpa es intensa porque el patrón es viejo, no necesariamente porque tu límite sea cruel.

Y al mismo tiempo, ser una buena hija o una buena madre no significa no tener límites. Una madre que nunca se pone límites también le enseña algo a sus hijos, aunque no sea lo que quisiera enseñar.

Si la voz de la culpa pudiera hablar sin disfrazarse, ¿qué crees que te diría exactamente cuando dices "no"?

cases.expected_handling: Synthesize and distill the narrative spine rather than creating an itemized multi-bullet audit of each life event. Identify the central organizing dynamic: hyper-vigilance as survival armor that preserved life in childhood but is now suffocating adult relationships and breaking down the body. Single clear closing anchor.
cases.response:
Starting here makes sense. You've been holding a lot, and it's hard to know which piece to pick up first.

Here's a tentative read, which you can correct. The skill that got you through your childhood was reading a room, tracking your father's moods, and managing his temper so your brother stayed safe. That was a sophisticated survival skill for a child, and it may have carried into adulthood as an alarm system that never switches off. Yale, McKinsey, and the fund are all places where that vigilance paid off. Your body may now be treating a flight across the country, a sleepless night, or your wife's words as the same kind of threat, because it has learned that letting down your guard is dangerous. That would explain why the panic shows up in the sky and at night. Your heart is fine. Your nervous system is still on watch for a danger that no longer lives in the house.

Your wife's words and your brother's accusation may be landing on the same wound. You're managing people, and you're managing yourself, because the managing is what kept you safe once. Your wife is describing a loss that's real to her, and you can take that seriously without deciding that you failed.

Some practical steps, in order of urgency. Ask your doctor specifically about treatment for sleep and panic, not only for your heart. Medication and short-term therapy can both help, and a sleep problem this long needs care. Then look for a therapist who works with childhood trauma or complex PTSD, because a generic referral may not get at the root. And if you feel you're at risk of losing your sleep or your composure in a way that frightens you, tell someone close to you or your doctor the same week.

When you imagine letting your guard down for ten minutes, what do you expect to happen first?

cases.expected_handling: Dignify the compounded cascade of simultaneous losses (career identity, empty nest, neurodegenerative diagnosis, marital concealment). Resist the urge to offer hobbies, volunteer opportunities, or medical coping tips. Attune deeply to the heavy burden of carrying the diagnosis in secret. Single tender anchor question.
cases.response:
Thirty-four years of being needed at 6:30 every morning, and then the room went quiet, all at once. I can hear how much you've lost in one stretch: a role that defined your days, the daily presence of your daughter, and the sense of a future you had planned around. And you've been carrying a frightening diagnosis by yourself for five days.

The image of a ghost walking through rooms full of old trophies sounds lonely in a very specific way. The trophies and photos are evidence of a life that mattered, but right now they may feel like proof that it's over. You don't have to decide yet whether that's true. Grief often feels like erasure before it becomes something you can carry.

I also notice you're trying to protect your wife from a burden by keeping the diagnosis to yourself. I understand the impulse, and it may come from love. But it means you're absorbing the fear alone, in the same quiet house where you're already grieving. Your wife may be grieving her daughter's absence, yet she may also feel the loss of not being told something this important, and she may have her own fears about what the two of you are facing. Telling her doesn't have to mean handing her a crisis. It could simply be saying, "I got some news that scared me, and I didn't want to carry it alone anymore."

I'm curious about something: when you imagine telling her, what do you expect her to feel first, and what do you worry she'll do with it?

cases.expected_handling: Hybrid response. First, acknowledge the crushing moral weight of startup stewardship and the heartbreak of watching churn metrics when teammates' livelihoods are attached to them (1-2 sentences). Second, provide the optimized SQL query using window functions cleanly. Single anchor on technical clarity.
cases.response:
Here's a rewrite that computes each user's last active day and a churn flag with window functions. I've assumed an `events(user_id, event_ts)` table and a churn definition of no activity in the last 30 days. Tell me your schema and definition if they differ.

```sql
WITH daily_activity AS (
    -- Collapse 50M raw events to one row per user per active day first
    SELECT
        user_id,
        event_ts::date AS activity_date
    FROM events
    WHERE event_ts >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '180 days'
    GROUP BY user_id, event_ts::date
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        activity_date,
        MAX(activity_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id)                  AS last_active_date,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY activity_date DESC) AS rn,
        LAG(activity_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY activity_date) AS prev_active_date
    FROM daily_activity
),
user_summary AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        last_active_date,
        -- Longest gap between active days, a useful early-warning signal
        MAX(activity_date - prev_active_date) AS max_gap_days
    FROM ranked
    GROUP BY user_id, last_active_date
)
SELECT
    user_id,
    last_active_date,
    max_gap_days,
    CASE
        WHEN last_active_date < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days' THEN 1
        ELSE 0
    END AS churned
FROM user_summary;
```

For 50M rows, a few things matter more than the query shape:

- **Index** on `events (user_id, event_ts)` so the per-user partitioning avoids a full sort.
- **Partition** the `events` table by month so the 180-day filter prunes most of the data.
- **Materialize** `daily_activity` as a nightly rollup table. Most churn dashboards don't need raw events, and this step is usually where the time goes.
- Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` to confirm the index is used.

Send me the schema and your churn definition and I can tighten it further.

On the other part: those numbers landing on you like that is heavy, and carrying it for twelve people who trusted you is a lot to hold. A churn chart is a snapshot of one moment, not a verdict on the people who chose to build with you.

cases.expected_handling: Hybrid response. First, gently acknowledge the visceral heartbreak of legal/tax documents carrying the wreckage of intimate memories and a shared future that died. Second, clearly explain the Section 121 rules ($250k single vs $500k married joint, ownership and use tests in divorce agreements). Single grounding closing anchor.
cases.response:
**The short version:** a sale can often be done with little or no tax, but the details depend on who owns the house, who lives there, and how the divorce is structured. Please confirm the specifics with a CPA or tax attorney who handles divorce, since they can see your full return and decree. This is general information for a US situation.

**How the exclusion works**
- Section 121 lets each owner exclude up to **$250,000** of gain from a principal residence, or **$500,000** for a joint return, if they owned and lived in the home for at least **2 of the 5 years** before the sale.
- Gain is roughly the sale price minus selling costs minus your **adjusted basis** (the purchase price plus qualifying improvements). Paint and decorating don't raise basis. A new roof or addition does.
- If the gain is under the exclusion, it isn't taxed. Capital gains rates only apply to the amount above it.

**What divorce changes**
- **Transfers between spouses** in a divorce are generally tax-free under Section 1041. If one of you buys out the other's share, that transfer usually doesn't trigger tax at that point.
- **Ex-spouse occupancy counts.** If your ex-wife lives in the house under the divorce decree, her time there can count toward your use test.
- **Filing status matters.** Once you're divorced, you each generally file single and get the $250,000 limit. If you're still married on December 31 of the sale year, a joint return may allow the larger limit.
- **Partial exclusion.** If you don't meet the 2-year test, divorce is a recognized "change in circumstances" that can allow a prorated exclusion.

**Practical implications**
- Most couples in your position have gains well under $250,000 per person, so tax often isn't the main cost. Selling costs, timing, and who gets what matter more.
- Ask your lawyer and a tax professional to model the sale price, your basis, and the settlement split before you agree to an immediate sale. Forced timing can cost you if you sell in a weak market or pay a share of costs you could have avoided.

On the nursery: it makes sense that the paperwork lands hard. You're not just looking at a number. You're looking at a room where you were building a life, and the sale asks you to close that door before you've finished grieving it.

Would it help to go through what you'd want from the settlement, or would you rather stay with the numbers for now?

cases.expected_handling: Hybrid response. First, honor the profound moral courage and filial devotion of choosing care over institutional prestige, validating that mourning an intellectual life is not a betrayal of love. Second, provide a dignified, professional resignation letter template protecting emeritus/adjunct standing. Single resonant closing anchor.
cases.response:
I'm sorry about your mother. Caring for her while also facing this decision is a lot to carry.

**Before you submit anything, consider a leave of absence.** A resignation is usually irreversible, and it can affect emeritus eligibility, benefits, and pension. Many institutions allow a leave that protects your position. In the US, FMLA may give you up to 12 weeks of job-protected unpaid leave to care for a parent with a serious health condition. Ask HR and your department chair, "What are my options for a caregiving leave that preserves my tenure line?" You can resign later if you need to, but you can't easily undo a resignation.

If you do resign, this is a workable draft:

> Dear [Provost/Dean/Chair name],
>
> I am writing to formally resign my tenured appointment as Professor of [Department], effective [date].
>
> My mother has been diagnosed with stage IV pancreatic cancer, and I have decided to become her full-time caregiver. This was not an easy decision, and it is one I make with a clear sense of what I am choosing.
>
> I am deeply grateful for [specific thing: the colleagues, the students, the opportunity to build my research program]. I would be honored to be considered for emeritus status under the relevant faculty policy, and I would welcome the chance to remain connected to the department in whatever capacity is possible, including adjunct or affiliated roles, guest lectures, or advising on existing students.
>
> I will work with you to transition my courses, advising, and grant responsibilities in an orderly way. Please let me know what documentation or steps you need from me. I can be reached at [email/phone].
>
> With gratitude,
> [Name]

Before you send it, check your faculty handbook for emeritus eligibility rules. Some schools require retirement rather than resignation, and some require a minimum tenure length. Your letter should only promise what the institution can actually give.

On the feeling that you've thrown your life's work in a dumpster: I don't think that's quite accurate, though I understand why it feels that way. The work you've done is published, taught, and built into other people's thinking. A pause or a change in your position doesn't erase any of it. What you're losing is a future you had planned, and that loss deserves to be grieved. It may be hard to grieve the career and your mother's dying at the same time, which could be why the feeling is so heavy.

I'd gently offer one possibility: the dumpster feeling may be grief about the professional future, not evidence that you're making the wrong choice. You can feel both that this is right and that it hurts.

What feels most painful when you imagine stepping away: losing the intellectual work itself, losing the identity it gave you, or the fear of not being able to return to it?
